newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislators urge more effective land use.
newsitem.headline: HK legislators urge more effective land use.

text.p: Hong Kong legislators on Thursday urged the government to stabilise hefty residential prices by raising supply through more effective use of land and other efforts to help speed up property development.
"In fact there may not be a shortage of land in Hong Kong. It's just that some land is not effectively used," Lee Wing-tat, chairman of the legislature's housing panel, told Reuters.
Lee was commenting on findings of a recent survey, conducted by the legislature, on the optimisation of land use.

The results showed that about 26.2 percent of the 4,972 hectares of land slated for residences under Hong Kong's current outline zoning plans and development permission area plans had a plot ratio -- or the ratio of gross floor area to net site area -- of one or below.
"And many rural areas have a low plot ratio of one or less," Lee noted.
Of the 1,003 hectares of residential land in rural areas, 96.4 percent had a plot ratio of one or less, the survey said.
Hong Kong home prices have been soaring in past months, up about 30 percent now from the end of last year, analysts said.
Rampant speculation and a shortage of supply in the face of rising demand have been blamed as the reasons for the rise.
Lee said the panel urged the government to boost housing supply by increasing plot ratios and turning farmland into residential sites.
The survey showed 6.6 percent of land in Hong Kong under the current plans is for agriculture, and 10.2 percent for residential development.
"We think farmland should be turned into residential land if Hong Kong does not need to develop agriculture," Lee said.

He also called for less government bureaucracy in procedures that have to be completed before a residential site is ready for development, saying red tape held up development projects and therefore slowed down housing supply.

Lee said the panel also urged for better infrastructural coordination to make sure residential projects could progress on schedule, and for more accurate population projections to ensure supply would meet demand.
The survey report noted the government had been underestimating population growth for over a decade.
"All land use plans are based on population projections, which have turned out to be too low in the past 15 years," the report said.
